full_judgment:
Sultan Hossain Khan, J.:—These two rules have arisen from the judgment and order of the Additional District Judge, Second Court, Comilla, affirming these of the learned Subordinate Judge, Chandpur passed in two Miscellaneous Cases under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act. 

 2. The pre-emptor opposite parties filed two applications for pre-emption under section 96 of the State Acquisition and Tenancy Act for pre-emption of two Kabala-lands appertaining to the holding under C.S. Khatian No 179 alleging that he was a co-sharer of the holding by way of gift from his father, In the application for pre-emption the pre-emptor imp leaded all the co-sharers of the holding as well as all the tenants of the lands contiguous to the Kabala-lands. In the pre-emption application the pre-emptor disclosed that he had applied for separation of the holding but he did not receive any khatian separating the holding as yet, and that as a precaution he bad imp leaded the tenants of the lands contiguous of the lands sought to be pre-empted. 

 5. Mr. Mujibur Rahman, the learned Advocate, appearing on behalf of the pre-emptee petitioner in both the rules, has submitted that the Courts below committed an error on an important question of law occasioning a failure of justice in allowing the amendments inasmuch as that the applications for pre-emption were filed by the pre-emptor claiming himself to be a co-sharer in the holding in question but by the impugned amendments be also claims pre-emption as an owner of the contiguous land and thus setting up new basis of his claim for pre-emption, and it has thus changed the character and nature of the cause of action which are not permissible under law. According to the learned Advocate the matter of evidence or fact may be supplemented or incorporated by way of amendment to support the basis of claim in a suit but introduction of a new claim by amending the foundation or basis of the claim as sought for, will alter the nature and character of the plaint or application and that the provisions of Order 6, rule 7 C.P.C. do not permit such amendment. He has further submitted that the original application for pre-emption was founded on the basis of the alleged right of the pre-emptor as a co-sharer but he nevertheless imp leaded all the owners of the contiguous land and it was done with a view to claim pre-emption on the basis that he was an owner of the land contiguous to the land of the kabala and at a time when the claim of the purchaser-pre-emptee under section 96(4) of State Acquisition & Tenancy Act for pre-emption, as a contiguous owner would be barred. The learned Advocate has further submitted that the impugned amendment of the application was mala fide. in that after the pre-emptee has filed the objection alleging that the holding had been. split up on the pre-emptor's own application for separation of the holding long before the filing of the application for pre-emption and the latter knew about it and thus the learned Additional District Judge committed a fundamental error in affirming the order of the trial Court as the application for amendment was clearly a mala fide one. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptee has next submitted that the omission of the pre-emptor to claim pre-emption in the application as a contiguous owner was initially malafide and motivated and as such amendment was erroneously allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge; further the learned Advocate has submitted the omission in the application to claim pre-emption was made to defeat the right of the pre-emptee as the contiguous owner of the kabala-lands. It has lastly been submitted that the court of appeal below committed a substantial error on a fundamental question of law in affirming the order of the learned Subordinate Judge in that the learned Subordinate Judge has acted illegally and without jurisdiction in allowing the amendments which have been prayed after the new cause of action or the claim has been barred by limitation and the pre-emptee has acquired a right against the pre-emptor vis-a-vis the pre-emptor's alleged claim of pre-emption on the basis as an owner of the land contiguous co the kabala-lands. The learned Advocate in support of his contention has referred io the decisions reported in P.L.D. 1963 (Dhaka) 87, 1960 P.L.D. (Lahore) 975, 17 DLR (S C.) 111, 15 DLR (SC) 120 and P L.D. 948 (PC) 73, 

 7. The two Kabalas sought to be pre-empted. in the two Miscellaneous Cases were registered under section 60 of the Registration Act on 30-9-8l and 30-10-81. The two application for pre-emption under section 96(1) of the S.A. & T. Act were filed on 25-11-81 on the basis that the pre-emptor was a co-sharer of the holding, and that they were within time. The pre-emptor imp leaded in his application all the co-sharers of the holding as well as all the tenants of the lands contiguous to the kabala-lands. Pre-emptor, however, stated in the application that he had applied for splitting up of the holding but he bad not received any khatian separating the holding. Though he imp leaded all the contiguous owners of the kabala-lands as parties to the proceeding, he did not claim pre-emption or the ground that he was also a contiguous were of the Kabala-land. After filing of the written objection by the pre-emptee that the original holding had been split up and a separate khatian had been created in the name of the pre-emptor in Mutation case No. 63 of 977-78 and that the pre-emptor was not a co-sharer of the holding and the applications for pre-emption were liable to be dismissed, pre-emptor prayed for amendment of the application on 20-4-82 claiming pre-emption alternatively as a tenant of the land contiguous to the lands transferred. 

 10. The. Supreme Court of India as well has disapproved alteration of the pleading as a result of which the his will assume a complexion wholly beyond the compass of the original cause of action (A.I.R. 1973) is 2110). In another decision date by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee petitioner namely, PLD 1963 (D) .87, a Division Bench of the High Court of Dhaka has disapproved an amendment of a plaint on the ground that the character of the claim has been totally changed by the amendment, and reversed the order of the trial Court allowing the amendment and rejected the petition for amend adieu. That case arose out of suit for specific performance of contract. The plaintiff alleged that he entered into an agreement with the defendant to purchase certain properties alleging payment of Tk. 6000/- as earnest money, out of the total consideration of Tk. 7000/- in presence of witnesses, and that the defendant put her L.T.I. on the receipt granted by her. The defendant filed a written statement denying the contract with her and payment of alleged earnest money in presence of the witnesses, and further alleging, he had been residing in Calcutta for the last 14 years, and that no such contract took place between her and the plaintiff. Upon filing :of such written statement the plaintiff filed an application for amendment of the plaint introducing that the contract had been entered into through her accredited Agent and authorised person, Premnath Banik. This petition for amendment was allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge On revision to the High Court against that order allowing the amendment their Lordships of the High Court disapproved the amendment and set aside the order. In that decision their Lordships has held the amendment which would totally change the character of the plaint though not of the suit and would prejudice the defendant should not be allowed. We do not it necessary to refer to the other cited by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee petitioner. 

 12. On the question of prejudice to the pre-empted, as has been pointed out by the learned Advocate for the pre-emptee, the amendment has been made at a time when his right to pre-emption as contiguous owner under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act has lapsed, and that the amendment has been done with a motive to defeat his right of pre-emption, The pre-emptor when he filed the application imp leaded. the tenants of the lands contiguous to the kabala-lands but in his pleadings he omitted to seek for pre-emption on the basis of a contiguous owner on the plea that he has not obtained a separate khatian splitting the holding, the pre-emptor has claimed his right of pre-emption on the basis that be is a co-sharer. We do not find any reason why in the original application he has not set up his claim as a contiguous owner of the disputed holding and limited his claim on the basis as a co-sharer only although undeniably the khatian has been split up well before the filing of the application for pre-emption. The learned Advocate for the pre-empty, purchaser has submitted that the omission to plead that the pre-emptor was a contiguous owner as well, has been made to defeat the claim of the pre-emptee under section 96(4) of the Act. The learned Advocate for the pre-empter, on the other hand, has submitted that in the objection against amendment no ground has been taken to the effect that the pre-emptee being a contiguous owner his right to pre-emption under section 96(4) has been defeated by reason of the subsequent amendment. In paragraph 7 of the application in this Court in both these Rules it has been stated that the pre-emptee is in possession of 3 sides of the disputed land. This statement has not been controverter before us by filing an affidavit. The learned Advocate for the pre-emptor however, has submitted that the pre-emptee is not a tenant of the land contiguous to the disputed land. 

 13. Be that as it may, we have found that the amendment of the applications as sought for by the pre-emptor bad changed the basis of the claim and consequently the complexion of the dispute. The claim of the pre-emptor for pre-emption on the basis that he is a contiguous owner of the kabala-lands is a fundamental alteration of the pleading and supplementing of an altogether new case. The impugned amendment has given a different complexion to the dispute between the parties which was beyond the compass of the original applications. We are therefore of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge has committed an error on an important question of law as to his power to grant or allow amendment of a pleading. The learned Subordinate Judge as well as the learned Additional District Judge has failed to notice that the amendment bad caused prejudice to the pre-emptee, the purchaser, in that he had no right of pre-emption under section 96(4) of the State Acquisition & Tenancy Act when the amendments were prayed for. The impugned amendments, in our view, ought not to have been allowed inasmuch as that if the applications for preempt ion as a co-sharer do not succeed, 'the claim for pre-emption on the basis of a contiguous owner of the Kabala-lands would be barred by limitation and as such the amendment should not have been allowed by the learned Subordinate Judge. As we have already referred to above, in the decision reported in 15 DLR. (SC) 120, their Lordships of the Supreme Court of Pakistan has held as follows:- 

 16. For the reason stated above we are of the view that the learned Subordinate Judge as well as the Court of appeal below committed an error of an important question of law in that they failed to exercise their judicial discretion in accordance with the correct principles to exercise the power of granting amendment under Order 6, rule 17 of the Code of Civil Procedure.
